1230.dq: One syllable in a phonological word is acoustically more prominent than all other syllables in the word, signalling that it carries primary stress. This syllable is pronounced with greater volume, a slight rise in pitch, and a lengthening of the vowel in the syllable nucleus.
1230.prule: Non-contrastive stress within a two-syllable right-edge window: in isolation a freestanding morpheme may be stressed freely on either the ultima or the penult (['ŋařan] ~ [ŋa'řan]); penult stress shifts one syllable rightward when monosyllabic suffixes/enclitics are added ([ŋa'řanto]); position also alternates ultima~penult depending on the identity of clitics in the phonological word ([man'čiddan] ~ [mančid'dan]). Author states the rules 'appear to be complex' and stress 'has not been fully analysed'.
1230.srule: Phonological words of four or more syllables carry a secondary stress, 'usually' on the second syllable to the left of the primary stress (ex. (4) ["ʔiʔḵa'nanto] 's/he will give something to someone'); only one secondary stress is described, iteration in longer words is not stated, and Brainard flags the stress system as 'not fully analysed'.
1230.quote: Phonological stress in Karao has not been fully analysed ... Secondly, there is evidence that stress is not contrastive, but predictable in Karao, although the exact rules for assigning stress appear to be complex. There are a number of empirical facts that point to this hypothesis: (a) There are no minimal pairs or near minimal pairs of words that contrast in stress only. (b) When a freestanding morpheme is pronounced in isolation, phonological stress can occur freely on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable; for example, the freestanding noun [ŋařan] 'name' may be pronounced ['ŋařan] …
1230.idn: Karao; data: villages in the Karao and Ekip barangays, municipality of Bokod, eastern Benguet, central Luzon, Philippines; data gathered March 1988 - March 1990 while the author lived in the village of Karao (SIL); c. 3,000 roots, speakers under and over forty
1230.exq_: A complete analysis of stress in Karao has yet to be undertaken; however, what is of importance for this study is that the phonological alternations described here occur in a syllable whether or not the syllable is stressed
1230.tone: No lexical tone; stressed syllable realised with greater volume, slight pitch rise and vowel lengthening.

1231.dq: A phonological word (see also §4.1.2 and §4.1.3) carries one main stress. Stress is manifested primarily by intensity and secondarily by length, stressed syllables on average being louder and longer than unstressed syllables.
1231.prule: Contrastive/lexical stress: unpredictable in disyllabic roots (minimal pairs, 129 initial vs 190 final among CVCVC); in roots of 3+ syllables stress falls on one of the last two syllables (mostly penult, many final), never initial; weight explicitly plays no role; with suffixes/enclitics stress tends to move to the rightmost stem syllable before the suffix/enclitic; author's analysis = tendency toward right-to-left trochee with residue unaccounted for.
1231.srule: Only in compounds and reduplications: a phonological word carries one main stress; secondary stress (same cues as primary, weaker) appears in some compounds, mainly numerals (non-final numeral keeps a secondary, e.g. 70 [put.ˌra.man.ˈda.lin]; (σ)σˈσσˌσ when the second member is disyllabic, e.g. [ɛs.ˈnɛm.tu.ˌmun]), and in reduplicated words of four or more syllables (primary usually on the second half, secondary on the other, e.g. /ˌsiŋaˈsiŋat/ 'ant', [ˌga.ruŋ.ˈga.ruŋ]; also [win.ˈjal.win.ˌjal]). None described in simple roots or affixed words; not rhythmic.

dfl.note: The author states an overall preference for penultimate stress (right-to-left trochee) covering roots of 3+ syllables, affixed words, compounds and reduplications; in disyllabic roots (the commonest root type) placement is explicitly unpredictable, with second-syllable (final) stress actually more frequent among CVCVC roots (190 vs 129).
dfl.q: By looking at roots longer than two syllables, as well as the effects of compounding, cliticisation and affixation on stress, it appears that Kalamang prefers stress on the penultimate syllable. Kalamang is therefore best analysed as having a tendency towards a trochaic foot structure (ˈσ.σ) assigned from right to left. This explains the penultimate stress in nearly all words carrying affixes.

1232.prule: Non-contrastive stress in a three-tone language; main stress falls on the stem (free-morpheme) syllable, and on the LAST syllable of a multisyllabic morpheme (iambic unstressed-stressed); prefixes unstressed; derivational suffixes count as part of the stem and may take main stress; inflection-like modal suffixes (realis, IRR1, IRR2) and enclitics are unstressed. Position is thus fixed by morpheme class (stem vs. prefix/inflectional suffix/clitic), not by syllable count from a word edge.
1232.srule: Exists, placement not given: Konnerth 2014 (sec. 3.6, translating Grüßner 1978: 23) mentions three stress grades -- 'in syllables with main stress and medium stress, tones are pronounced clearly. In syllables with weak stress, tones become indistinguishable' -- but gives no rule for where medium (secondary) stress falls; Konnerth's own description is binary stressed/unstressed (iambic within the morpheme) and defers a phonetic study of stress to future work.

1235.prule: Stress falls preferentially on 'strong' syllables, strength being defined segmentally: front and back (peripheral) vowels are strong, central vowels weak; labial/velar consonants (esp. mp, nk) and CC clusters (esp. tn.quote: Three levels of pitch occur phonetically in Karo words: high, mid and low. Of these, only high and low are phonologically contrastive; mid pitch is the phonetic realization of low pitch in stressed syllables. Since high, mid and low pitches do not rise or fall during their production, the pitch system of Karo can be categorized as a 'register level pitch system' (Pike 1948). Furthermore, the fact that only high and mid pitches occur in stressed syllables, and that high and mid pitches are also used to distinguish the meanings of words make Karo a 'pitch-accent' language (Hyman 1975).

tn.note: Two contrastive level pitches, high vs low (mid = low under stress); one underlying high per word, which attracts stress; Gabas calls Karo a 'pitch-accent' language. H/M spreads rightward.

1244.dq: The phonological word (PW) functions within the higher phonological phrase and provides a useful construction for specifying underlying stress and syllable patterns.
1244.prule: Lexically contrastive stress on a right-edge two-syllable window: every phonological word (1-3 syllables) belongs to one of two 'contrastive classes', ultimate stress ((S)S)Ś or penultimate stress (S)ŚS; class membership is not predictable (e.g. /u.dí/ 'banana', /mi.á/ 'mother' ultimate vs /bÁ.nu/ 'moon', /glú.ik/ 'to bail' penultimate). Note 7 (p.60) counts the two CA.CVC stress shapes at 220 (24%) and 150 (17%) of 900 words; the accent marks that distinguish the two lines are not legible in the scan, but note 6, which is anchored to the statement that stressed /A/ 'is almost always [a]' (p.46) and is illustrated only with penultimate-stress forms (/kló.paŋ/, /kém.tuik/, /to.gó.li/, /de.mé.niŋ/), gives 'CA.CVC occurs 220 times', so 220 (24%) is the penultimate-stress shape CÁ.CVC and 150 (17%) the ultimate-stress shape CA.CV́C. 1246.prule: One stressed syllable per word; in verb forms the verb stem is always stressed (regardless of prefixes such as ʔi-, mu-, mʌ-), i.e. stress position is fixed by morphological structure, not syllable count or weight. A two-way tonal contrast (level vs falling) is realized only on the stressed syllable and neutralized on unstressed/short vowels.

Jacques 2016 sec. 2 instead states that verbs and nouns alike have only one stressed syllable (compound verbs excepted). No rhythmic secondary stress is described.

In verb forms, the verb stem is always stressed, as is the first syllable of a bi- or tri-syllabic suffix string. Given its predictable nature in verb forms, stress is not indicated in the present paper. ... [Jacques 2016 sec. 2] Khaling has a two-way tonal contrast on open syllables with long vowels or closed syllables with a sonorant coda. There is a high level tone (indicated by a macron) and a falling tone (circumflex accent). ... The tonal contrast is neutralized on short and / or unstressed vowel…

1246.tone: Two-way lexical/morphological tone (high level vs falling; marginal low level in the purposive -bi construction) contrastive only on long-vowel open syllables or sonorant-coda syllables, and only on the stressed syllable of a polysyllable (Jacques 2016; Jacques et al. 2012). Toba 1979 describes it as two word tones (high/low) carried on the first syllable and determined by the stem. The system is thus stress + culminative tone (word-tone/pitch-accent-like), not tone without stress.

morph.elicq: No evidential basis is given for the stress statement itself: 'Given its predictable nature in verb forms, stress is not indicated in the present paper' (2012 p.1100). The data in general come from paradigm elicitation: 'The data presented here were collected in July 2011, by a team of linguists during a month of intensive elicitation and discussion with Dhan Bahadur Rai in Paris, and in early 2012 by Guillaume Jacques during two months of fieldwork in Kathmandu and in the district of Solu Khumbu' (2012 p.1097); no instrumental study of stress is reported in any source.
morph.stmt: Predominantly suffixing with one prefixal slot: 'There are one prefixal position and seven suffixal positions' in the finite verb template (Jacques et al. 2012 p.1101, Table 3); 'Kiranti morphology is mainly suffixal... 1249.prule: Reconstructed word stress for an extinct language (evidence: vowel palatalization only in stressed syllables, weakening/loss in unstressed syllables, and metrical ictus). Emmerick 2024 marks one stress per word and says nothing about secondary stress. tn.translation: The presence of tones is extremely probable: in Late Khotanese many words (syllable-morphemes) are marked with a special sign, rendered in transliteration as _ [the subscript hook]; in these syllables a hushing sibilant or r dropped out in pre-Khotanese, and in some cases in Early Khotanese, sometimes a neighbouring syllable was also syncopated. Presumably a pharyngealized tone, or a kind of prosodic 'erization', can be reconstructed for them. Such a reconstruction is areally supported by the neighbourhood of Chinese, Tibetan and Uyghur and by living attested contacts with them.

1250.dq: All Bs speech varieties except some dialects of Kuy and Tsg retain phonemic accent. ... In all dialects stress is a syntactic feature, a means of counting the full words in a clause ...; it does not always coincide with length. The typical stress pattern of a word can be overridden by certain intonation patterns.

1251.dq: When it comes to stress, Kinyarwanda has been observed to show both word penultimate and phrase penultimate lengthening (Myers 2005), which is reminiscent of what is found in other Bantu languages.

1251.prule: Tone language: privative High vs toneless (0) contrast, mora = TBU; lexical H may fall on any stem syllable of a noun (one lexical H per morpheme), verbs take H on stem syllable 1 or 2 by lexical/grammatical assignment; tones also mark morphology and syntax. No word-stress rule is stated by the primary; the only stress-like property reported (secondary, after Myers 2005) is phonetic penultimate lengthening at word and phrase level.

evidence_works.detail: The thesis treats Rwanda first-hand in its group II (Hautes Terres de l'Ouest) and classifies it by its own criterion of tone-pattern counts on disyllabic stems: '"(a): 5, (b): 2": shi (groupe I); rwanda/rundi, hangaza ?, shubi ?, ha ? (groupe II)' (p. 79; languages with (a) between 1 and 4 are his 'langues à accent'). Sec. 5.2.1 (p. 189): 'ces deux langues ne sont pas des langues à accent d'après notre définition: en effet, si les thèmes nominaux §cvcvç ne présentent bien que trois schèmes tonals sous-jacents... les thèmes de forme §cvvcvç eux en présentent cinq'; and the H of a mora 's'associe non seulement à celle-ci, mais aussi, et ce en toutes circonstances, à la more précédente' (p. 190, tone anticipation). Sec. 5.2.5 (pp. 200-201; the text has no 5.2.6, 5.3.1 follows): treating the language as accentual with default L 'nous est, hélas, interdit par les quatre schèmes de thèmes nominaux dissyllabiques', so Rwanda/Rundi form 'un groupe de langues en transition vers un système accentuel'. P. 252: 'le rwanda-rundi (groupe II) où l'opposition tonale existe dans le lexique, mais est neutralisée à la plupart des tiroirs'. P. 462: Rwanda/Rundi are the group that merged HH with BH rather than HB. The thesis does not state any stress rule, penultimate lengthening or demarcative accent for Rwanda (no 'allongement' or 'accent démarcatif' passage names it; the demarcative penultimate accent near the Rwanda-Rundi paragraph, p. 413, is about Nyoro/Tooro). The typology of penult-bound tone processes (sec. 3.5.2, pp. 485-486) lists rwanda-rundi among languages where a final H 's'en dissocie devant pause absolue' (p. 485) and where 'un H final est rétracté sur la' 'deuxième more d'une syllabe pénultième longue et entièrement B' (p. 486); p. 435 groups 'shi, rwanda, jita' as examples of a long penultimate vowel attracting a final H; p. 413 states that shubi, hangaza and probably ha 'partagent le sytème tonal du rwanda-rundi'. These are tone rules keyed to the penult, not a stress rule or lengthening, so they leave the coding unchanged.

evidence_works.detail: Two-level system: “On the lexical and morphosyntactic levels, every vowel is either Hi (marked by an acute accent) or Lo (unmarked). The opposition between Hi and Lo is lexically distinctive” (sec. 1.2.2, p. 6; minimal pairs inda ‘belly’ / indá ‘louse’, umuryaango ‘family’ / umuryáango ‘door’, guhera ‘grind’ / guhéra ‘stay away’). Tone is assigned per mora; a long vowel with Hi+Lo morae is called falling, Lo+Hi rising. Vowel length is distinctive (sec. 1.2.1.2). Restricted domain: verb roots are Hi or Lo with the Hi on the first stem mora “no matter how long the stem is”; nouns take a front Hi

1253.prule: Kiowa is a register-tone language (high and low tonemes, plus a high+low falling combination, on the syllable; vowel length also contrastive). Stress is non-contrastive: it varies freely and is only statistically conditioned by tone (high and falling syllables attract stress), vowel length, and vowel openness; no positional word-stress rule.
1253.srule: Not mentioned in Sivertsen 1956 (sec. 6 'Stress', pp. 125-126, read in full with secs. 0-4 and 9): stress as a whole is non-contrastive and freely fluctuating ('Two utterances of the same word may show different stress patterns'); no primary/secondary distinction and no rhythmic stress is posited.
1253.quote: 6. Stress. Stress is also non-contrastive. It may vary freely without causing ambiguity, but it is generally conditioned by one or more of several factors. If stress is defined in terms of acoustical pressure as measurable by a continuous level recorder or on a cathode-ray oscillograph, the following relations have been observed: a. An open vowel is generally more stressed than a close one. ... b. A /high/ syllable is in general more stressed than a /low/ one. ... In the following words it is the /high/ syllable which carries the heaviest stress, irrespective of its place within the word ... …

Harrington 1928 section 9 writes high/low 'pitch accent' on pronominal prefixes only.

tn.quote: In addition to the segmental phonemes listed above, Kituba employs stress and pitch differences. While not normally considered a tone language, Kituba does have a number of pairs of words the sole distinction between the members of which is a matter of stress and pitch. ... Thus it would appear that in these forms Kituba has words in which a feature of tone (pitch) is phonemic. The grammatical function of such tonal differences is zero and the number of pairs of words on which this feature operates is relatively low

tn.note: Penultimate 'word accent' = pitch rise (root vowel also long); a few words (Lingala loans, e.g. kusŏlula 'converse' vs kusōlúla 'find') lack it, so pitch is marginally phonemic; no tone inventory.

1256.cfw: Swift and Zola 1963 describe a fixed word accent, a pitch rise on the next-to-last syllable regardless of word length, for the Brazzaville-type Kituba this record covers, and Mufwene 2009 independently calls the system a predominantly fixed penultimate accent, while the only dissent, Ngalasso 1991, describes the eastern Bandundu variety of the DRC, treats the penultimate pitch rise there as lexical tone beside a root-initial length accent, and himself concedes that Brazzaville speech sounds strongly accentual and that Lumwamu 1983 analyses Munukutuba as a penultimate-accent language.
